newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawyer says liquor, airline mergers may be tied.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawyer says liquor, airline mergers may be tied.

text.p: A prominent antitrust lawyer said Tuesday the United States may weigh Europe's handling of the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger in deciding whether to interevene in the marriage of liquor giants Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc.
"In making that decision a lot of foreign relations and diplomatic concerns come into the equation," said Lloyd Constantine of Constantine Partners in New York.

Constantine said that some in the American government may look at the European Union's handling of the merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. in deciding whether to intervene in the $15.8 billion liquor merger.
Both the United States and the European Union would have jurisdiction over the two European liquor companies, which sell heavily in the United States.

"I can foresee a situation where if the Europeans press forward on the air manufacturing merger someone will suggest we get involved in the (liquor merger)," he said. "I think that the use of antitrust investigations to potentially stop mergers which are primarily occurring in other countries is now an additional weapon in the trade war arsenal."
But Constantine said the decision will be up to the government, not private parties.
A competing liquor company, Seagram Co. Ltd., on Monday attacked the merger as anticompetitive and suggested there would be antitrust concerns.
Stephen Axinn, of the antitrust firm of Axinn, Veltrop & Harkrider in New York, disagreed about whether the United States would become involved in the Guiness merger.
"I'm sure the government will look at it," he said. "How the European Community chooses to define its jurisdiction is interesting but not conclusive."

Axinn said the companies would have a very strong position in the blended Scotch business. If the two liquor companies "were to create a monopoly in the blended Scotch business then the United States could clearly act," he said.
Axinn speculated that the merging companies could solve their problems by divesting the Scotch labels.
He said that the stills and equipment themselves might not have to be divested, because the question was one of barriers to new entrants into the field.

Axinn said that because the major U.S. television networks are still refusing to run liquor advertising, it might be difficult for a new major brand in blended Scotch whisky to become established within two years. The two-year test is used by antitrust authorities.
